full_judgment: 74. In civil cases, while deciding applications relating to matters of injunction, the Court takes into account the "balance of convenience and inconvenience" of the parties while granting or rejecting the prayer for injunction. Similarly, in criminal cases, when the prosecution witnesses, being blood relatives of the deceased, tender obliging depositions favouring the accused person and are consequently declared hostile by the prosecution, in such event, their evidence should be judged having regard to the "degree of probability or improbability." In order words, the deposition of a prosecution witness, being a blood relative of the victim, who has been declared hostile by the prosecution, must be assessed very critically to determine the veracity of such statement. It is appears that the deposition of that witness is grossly inconsistent with or contrary to the prosecution story and other evidence on record, in such event, the deposition of that particular witness has to weighted having regard to a "decree of probability or improbability". It has to be seen whether it was probable and likely that such witness was giving false and misleading evidence in Court in order to shield the accused persons or whether it was improbable and unlikely for the incident to have taken place in the manner as disclosed by such witness. This 'degree of probability or improbability" of the deposition of any particular witness should be the guiding factor in assessing the veracity of the deposition of that particular witness.
